#5705. Mobile Energy Hubs: How Chery Auto’s Smart Energy Ecosystem Supports the Development of Smart Cities Worldwide

WUHU, China — Following the 2026 Chery International User Summit, Chery Auto is pressing ahead with its new energy ecosystem strategy. Entering the Globalization 3.0 phase, the company is deploying a mix of energy solutions to meet mobility energy needs around the world. As electric vehicles integrate with power grids, Chery Auto is developing a smart energy ecosystem that transforms new energy vehicles (NEVs) into dispatchable distributed mobile energy nodes, supporting grid management, sustainable urban development, and local energy resource utilization.

Unlike conventional charging, which can increase peak demand, V2G offers a flexible alternative. Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) enables bidirectional flow, allowing vehicles to store off-peak electricity and return power during peak demand. For users, this creates opportunities to participate in energy management and potentially generate value. With participation depending on commercial feasibility and user confidence, Chery Group’s global user base exceeding 21 million provides a foundation for V2G deployment.

Chery Auto is validating its energy ecosystem across homes, communities and industrial parks. Its household Energy Cube integrates solar, storage and bidirectional charging to support electricity supply during exceptional conditions. In Wuhu, a large-scale AC V2G demonstration station enables private vehicles to support grid management through onboard chargers with limited modifications. In Spain, an industrial park microgrid uses green electricity to reduce energy costs, fossil fuel dependence, and carbon emissions.

Chery Auto’s Volt-dragon Ultra-Fast Charging technology targets 500 km of range in five minutes. Its hybrid engine has achieved 48.57% thermal efficiency, while the planned Rhino S solid-state battery targets 400 Wh/kg energy density. Chery’s Rhino Battery prioritizes fast charging, longevity and safety, addressing battery degradation and thermal management concerns associated with V2G charging cycles.

Chery Auto is developing modular solar, storage, charging, and V2G solutions tailored to regional infrastructure. In Europe, electricity markets provide opportunities for distributed energy participation. Mature markets integrate vehicles into grid management, while regions with weaker infrastructure can prioritize microgrids before introducing V2G.

Through applications spanning households, communities, and industrial parks, Chery Auto is extending automotive-grade engineering into energy infrastructure. Its approach supports distributed energy networks using locally generated electricity and managing energy flows, positioning Chery to participate in future smart cities.

#5704. Are Collectors Overpaying For These Japanese Sports Cars?

If you've been paying close attention to the collector car market in recent years, particularly since 2020, you've likely noticed that many golden era Japanese cars have started going for big bucks. Wealthy Gen X and millennial enthusiasts are pushing this nostalgia-fueled, Gran Turismo-inspired market well past what anyone might have thought possible in years gone by. With six-figure price tags no longer out of the ordinary, perhaps it's time to put a finger on the market's pulse and dig into the forces driving these massive prices. Are these cars really worth the spend, and will they continue to hold value into the future? It's tough to say for sure, but I'll give it my best shot.

Considering the comparative mass-market production numbers of some of these Japanese classics, maybe there isn't enough rarity for these cars to command the numbers they do. Then again, these are some of the greatest cars of their eras, and no automaker on the planet makes anything today that can compete on a level playing ground with the best of years gone by. Perhaps these values are just a combination of "They just don't make them like they used to" and "They aren't making any more of them."

At the end of the day, cars are only worth what someone is willing to pay for them, and in each of these cases it seems there are plenty of people willing to spend what it takes to buy them. Surely there are plenty of fools quick to part with their money, and there always will be. Some of these premium prices, however, are getting out of hand. Let's pump the brakes a little and get realistic about what collectors are actually getting for their cash.

I've spilled plenty of ink and burned plenty of internet pixels extolling the virtues of the flip-up-headlight Acura NSX. This is an incredible car and the driving experience is sublime. Perhaps the only problem with the NSX, especially now that Acura has started to reproduce many of the components needed to keep one alive, is that it's too good. The NSX doesn't have the sound or the fizz many of its Italian or German competitors from the era do. In that respect it's perhaps a little on the sterile side. It's so well-engineered that it just does everything you expect it to, which can't always be said of those competitors.

The long and short of this car is that I love it dearly, and I kind of understand why people are willing to spend deep into the hundreds of thousands of dollars for one. According to Hagerty, a #1 conscours-condition car is valued at a quarter of a million on the high end. This is borne out in recent Bring A Trailer auction results, with 10 red first-gen NSXes selling in October alone, ranging from $72,000 on up to $156,000 for a low-mile example. In many cases that's on par with, or even more than, Bring A Trailer's current sales prices of its contemporary Ferrari 348 competitors.

Between 1991 and the end of NSX production in 2004, U.S. sales added up to 8,733 cars, and about 18,000 worldwide. That's actually quite rare, all things considered, but there are always a few available. Buy a high-mile driver-grade NSX at a discount and keep driving it. These things are best once they've worn in a little.

When Datsun debuted the 240Z in the late 1960s as a bargain-priced competitor to the premium European sports cars of the day, it was wildly successful and helped cement the brand's place in the U.S. market. Why spend so much more for a Porsche 911 when a Datsun offered a similar level of performance and head-turning good looks? All these decades later, the 240Z is still a great low-priced vintage alternative to a vintage 911. Today the price gap is perhaps even higher between the German and the Datsun, though the maintenance and aftermarket parts support for both has continued to narrow.

Hagerty claims a #1 condition 240Z will command up to $181,000 at auction, but I don't think anything near that is even close to accurate. I've seen perfectly restored examples trade hands recently for as little as $50,000, and driver-grade units sell on Bring A Trailer every couple of weeks for between 20 and 45 grand. Whatever your budget, and whatever your stomach for tinkering, there's a 240Z out there for you.

Between 1969 and 1973 Nissan shipped 168,584 of these great little machines around the world. The vast majority of them (nearly 90%) ended up in the U.S., largely due to Europe's restrictive post-World War II trade embargoes. It's hard to call a 240Z overpriced, simply by dint of how many were built. There are plenty out there to sate collector demand, and prices reflect that. If you want one, go for it. As with any old car, beware of rusty, poorly restored cars, or any with a checkered past, as you'll pay more to fix one with issues than the premium for a nice one.

I am a Honda S2000 sycophant, convinced that this is the best driving experience that money can buy. If the Mazda Miata is always the answer, then the S2000 is the path to enlightenment. The early cars with an 8,800-rpm-redline 2.0-liter four-cylinder are pure driving joy. This is exhilaration, verve, and direct feel distilled to its most pure and uncut. If you've never driven one, you'll never understand it. Unlike the NSX, the S2000 is all fizz and very little usability. It's not great on the highway, isn't particularly comfortable, and has no room for anything. It was built to make you feel something, and that's pretty much all it can do. It's a real one-trick pony, but that trick is sublime.

Hagerty pegs a perfect condition AP1 at just over $64,000, up 22% from three years ago. Real-world sales on Bring A Trailer show buyers tapping out at $50,000 on the high end, with nice driver-grade examples down in the low 20s. If you look you might be able to find some in the high teens.

It's hard to call the S2000 rare, as Honda built over 110,000 of these little screamers across 11 years of production. I prefer the models built from 1999 to 2003; they're a little lighter, rev higher and the handling is more like balancing on the edge of a knife. Honda built far more AP1 versions of the car than it did the later 2.2-liter AP2 models, as 72,684 of the former made it out into the world. I don't think these will ever be purely collectible, just on the sheer number built, so don't pay a premium for a #1 example. Buy a nice driver and enjoy miles on twisty roads and track days.

As enthusiastic as I am about Honda's ripper S2000, I remain perplexed by the stratospheric growth of JZA80 Toyota Supra Turbo love. Aside from its role as the star of "The Fast And The Furious" and some highly modified examples, it's an entirely underwhelming ownership experience. Toyota designed the fourth-generation Supra around subframes, suspension, and drivetrain assemblies from the Z30-generation Soarer (sold in the U.S. as the Lexus SC), meaning it's a highly competent, comfortable grand tourer, but a sports car it is not. If you're after a high-speed long-legged highway cruiser, it's pretty great, but it doesn't really feel special to drive.

There's something to be said for above-average ergonomics and a practically indestructible engine wrapped in simple, attractive bodywork? Of course, but is it a driving experience worth up to $297,000? According to Hagerty, a concours condition Supra could bring that sum at auction. I can't recall having seen one trade hands for quite that much recently, but there are plenty of examples deep into the six figures, like this low-mile unit that went unsold on Bring A Trailer after a high bid of $209,000.

In every case I'd personally rather have a C5-generation Corvette, offering more power and more twisty-road-ready driving character for orders of magnitude less money. I'm excited that Japanese cars have been grabbing collector attention for the last couple of decades, but I'm positive you can find better cars offering more excitement behind the wheel than this. Japan, and indeed Toyota, has built better grand tourers and better sports cars (and cars that are better at both) since this car exited production.

The Acura Integra Type R is perhaps the car that best exemplifies the overpriced Japanese collector car. Don't get me wrong, this is a magnificent machine with legendary driving character, but at its core it's a pumped-up economy car. Even though it's possibly the best front-wheel-drive experience, and punches well above its weight, it seems downright offensive that these occasionally command six- figure price tags. It's got all the incredible characteristics of a fast Honda, including the reliability, tight steering, and wonderful shifter feel. It also comes with the downsides of a loud, buzzy interior, aesthetically underwhelming design, and a lack of low-end torque. It's a lot of fun on a track or a twisty road, but not a very nice daily driving experience.

According to the Hagerty valuation tool, an Integra Type R in concours condition can expect to bring around $99,000 at auction on the high end. This one seems to actually be underselling the highs of the Integra market, as Bring a Trailer results show. Last summer a low-mile ITR traded hands for $204,204. While nothing has reached that high since, a 19,000-mile example sold for $88,500 in October. Many of these cars have a checkered past, as Integras were once the most stolen car in America, so if you find one with high miles or a rebuilt title, you can probably get the same driving experience for a major discount. A driver-grade car seems to sell in the $20,000-to-$30,000 range.

If you're looking for a less expensive high-revving, great-handling front-wheel-drive economy-based car that works great when the road gets curvy, maybe try a Dodge Neon ACR instead. I put my money where my mouth is a couple years ago, and I never had any ITR jealousy.

There are plenty of other cars from Japan in this conversation, but I don't think this is an intrinsically Japanese collector car problem. In fact, cars from Japan tend to be overlooked by collectors, and have been for decades. There are plenty of reasons to buy a Japanese sports car, but as the market continues to trend upward, many enthusiasts are getting priced out of their dream cars. Still, some, perhaps even many, Japanese cars are still worth the money they command on the used market, especially in light of the lack of choices and driver connectivity in the new car market.

I typically don't like to talk about collector car values, because it continues to prop up the cars-as-commodities trading industry. Buy what you love and what makes you feel good, and drive the wheels off the thing. What's the point in having a car if you aren't going to drive it as it was meant to be driven? You don't get emotion or experience from storing value in your garage. Perhaps more than any other car-building nation, Japan understands experience and the interconnectedness between driver and machine.

If you're buying one of these cars because you're expecting it to go up in value and make you money, perhaps you'd be better served investing in the stock market or betting on the ponies. Cars are passion and craftsmanship, and they need to be driven to extract their full value to humanity. Go to a car show, a track day, or take one on a long road trip with friends. There are smiles to be found in those miles. Buy what makes you happy.

#5703. Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer

Men with very low testosterone levels may face an increased risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease later in life, according to a major international study. The findings suggest that testosterone levels could provide an early clue to future health risks, potentially years or even decades before cancer is diagnosed.

Researchers found that men with low testosterone had an 18 percent higher risk of dying from cancer. However, the relationship was not the same for every type of cancer. Surprisingly, testosterone levels were not associated with prostate cancer risk. Instead, prostate cancer was more closely linked to low levels of two other hormones, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and luteinizing hormone.

The research comes from the Androgens In Men Study (AIMS), an international collaboration led by Professor Bu Yeap at The University of Western Australia. The project investigates how different sex hormones relate to cancer risk and other health outcomes in men.

Study Tracks Testosterone and Cancer Risk in 26,000 Men

Published in the journal Lancet Healthy Longevity, the study examined data from more than 26,000 men participating in 11 long-running studies across Australia, the United States, and Europe.

Researchers analyzed hormone concentrations in blood samples collected earlier in the men's lives. They then compared those measurements with cancer diagnoses and deaths recorded over the following decades, allowing them to investigate whether hormone levels were associated with future cancer outcomes.

The analysis included testosterone, dihydrotestosterone (DHT), SHBG, and luteinizing hormone. Luteinizing hormone is produced by the pituitary gland and signals the testes to produce testosterone.

"We wanted to know whether the concentration of these hormones in the blood was related to the risk of men being diagnosed with, or dying from, cancer into the future," Professor Yeap said.

"What we saw was that if a man had low testosterone levels - in the lowest one-fifth compared to the highest one-fifth of the range - their subsequent risk of dying from cancer was higher, even after allowing for age and other health-related factors."

Cancer Risk Increased Below a Key Testosterone Level

The researchers identified a testosterone concentration below which cancer risk began to rise. According to Professor Yeap, testosterone levels in healthy younger men typically range from 10 to 30 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L), although concentrations generally decrease with age.

Testosterone levels can also be influenced by factors that people may be able to change, including body mass index and physical activity. Certain medical conditions, such as diabetes, can affect testosterone concentrations as well.

"We saw that when baseline testosterone was below 8.6 nmol/L, subsequent cancer risk started increasing," Professor Yeap said.

"This suggests low testosterone is an important biomarker, so it's possible that looking at testosterone levels could help us identify men who might do poorly if they get cancer down the track."

These findings raise the possibility that testosterone measurements could help doctors recognize men who may face greater health risks in the future. However, the results show an association and do not establish that low testosterone itself causes cancer.

A Surprising Finding About Prostate Cancer

Because testosterone plays an important role in male reproductive health, researchers also investigated whether naturally occurring testosterone levels influenced the likelihood of developing prostate cancer.

The question has particular medical significance because lowering testosterone is an established treatment for prostate cancer. However, the new analysis found no evidence that a man's natural testosterone concentration was associated with his risk of developing the disease.

"Since reducing testosterone levels is a treatment for prostate cancer there's always been a question of whether the amount of testosterone your own body makes relates to your risk of prostate cancer but based on our findings there's no evidence they are related," Professor Yeap said.

"We did find, however, that men with low levels of SHBG and luteinizing hormone were at higher risk of prostate cancer."

The results highlight an important distinction between testosterone and other hormones involved in male reproductive function. Although low testosterone was associated with higher overall cancer risk and mortality, prostate cancer showed a different pattern of hormonal associations.

Why Low Testosterone Does Not Mean Men Need Supplements

Despite the connection between low testosterone and cancer outcomes, Professor Yeap emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation to take testosterone supplements to prevent cancer.

"While we've shown low levels are associated with increased risk, we haven't got any evidence yet that actually giving men testosterone will reduce that risk," he said.

Instead, unexpectedly low testosterone could be a reason to investigate a person's overall health. A medical evaluation may uncover underlying conditions or risk factors that require attention, even when there is no evidence of a problem affecting the testes.

"What we would say to men is if they are found for whatever reason to be low in testosterone, it's important to go to the doctor for a full checkup. It may not show any sign of testicular disease, but it might show other health issues or risk factors they need to address.

"It could be a wake-up call and encouragement for men to engage in more healthy lifestyle behaviors, and to get regular, holistic checkups to stay on top of their health."

Materials provided by University of Western Australia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5702. Trump Admin Pauses Enforcement of Its Medicaid Work Rules

— States have gotten a reprieve from the looming January 1 deadline

President Donald Trump's administration told states Friday that they can wait until July before removing people from Medicaid for failing to meet a work requirement.

The requirement is scheduled to take effect nationally on Jan. 1, 2027, and states have been scrambling to put in place the staffing, training, and technology to implement it by then. The administration clarified that while states still have the option to take action at the beginning of the year, they won't have to kick anyone off or deny coverage for failure to meet the requirement until July 1.

Medicaid is the joint state-federal health insurance program for lower-income people. CMS told state Medicaid directors on Friday that they'll still need to determine whether many enrollees and applicants for benefits are meeting new requirements that they are working, in school, or volunteering.

The move announced Friday gives state social service departments more time to make sure complicated changes are ready to run before there are consequences. CMS said that states are making progress but have implementation challenges.

"I think these extra 6 months are going to give states the ability to respond to the change, and there will be fewer people that lose their coverage due to administrative failures" resulting from states' inability to prepare, Kathy Hempstead, senior policy officer for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, told AP.

Still, she said it's not clear which states will opt to use the additional time.

Kate McEvoy, executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors, said state Medicaid leaders "appreciate the additional flexibility that CMS is providing."

The decision also could give some breathing room to Congress to consider changes to the requirement. Democrats who are taking control of both chambers in January after their sweeping election victories last week have said they want to roll back the requirements.

The news comes after Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), and Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (D-NJ) wrote to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, MD, MBA, this week, asking to delay implementing the work reporting requirements. Their letter cites, in part, a recent decision out of a Boston federal court that determined medically frail people should not be bound by the work requirement qualification rules.

"The practical reality is that this significant implementation issue may not be definitively resolved for months, creating untenable uncertainty for states that need a final resolution of this issue before going live with work reporting requirements," the letter states. "The court ruling is an important victory for the millions of medically frail people who rely on Medicaid for their healthcare coverage."

Under the policy, many Medicaid beneficiaries must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month or be in school at least half-time. The new policy applies only to people who receive Medicaid under a voluntary expansion that 40 states undertook and which was intended to get health coverage to more lower-income adults who don't have kids at home. There are exceptions for those who are over age 64, caring for kids under age 14 years, or deemed too medically frail to work.

Critics say that most enrollees covered by the mandate are already working and that people are more likely to lose coverage because of the paperwork to prove it rather than failing to work.

The federal government is pushing states to use data from other government departments or elsewhere to verify whether beneficiaries are working as a way to reduce the burden on the beneficiaries to show proof.

A few states have launched the work requirements early.

The first of them was Nebraska, where they started in May.

Preliminary data presented to the state's Medicaid Advisory Committee showed that more than nine in 10 people subject to the work requirement and due to have their benefits renewed in July and August qualified.

But 533 people were denied continuing coverage. For most of them, it was over paperwork: They didn't show that they were working or were exempt from the requirement. Of those denied, 43 lost coverage because they did not meet the new requirement.

Similarly, most of the new Medicaid applicants who were denied coverage due to work requirements from May through August did not get the coverage because they did not provide information to verify whether they were complying.

Among both groups, it's not clear how many people didn't provide information because they weren't working -- or how many might meet the requirements but failed to show it.

"There are likely people who are still eligible for coverage who lost it," said Amy Behnke, CEO of the Health Care Center Association of Nebraska.

#5701. Patient experience has improved across the healthcare industry. Now comes consistency

Patient experience has improved across the healthcare industry. Now comes consistency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient experience metrics collected over millions of encounters show continuous topline improvements across all types of care settings, either meeting or surpassing those reported ahead of the pandemic.

But the gains aren’t uniform, with substantial variation between organizations, regions, patient groups, admission types, specialty and other operational factors under providers’ control, warned Qualtrics in its “State of Patient Experience 2026” report, released Thursday.

“The national trendline is encouraging, but tells an incomplete story,” the report reads. “Some organizations are improving rapidly; others are standing still.”

The experience management software vendor’s analysis, released Thursday, pulled data from 43.1 million of its over 2,500 hospitals and 490,000 medical office site customers.

It showed national patient experience scores like Likelihood to Recommend (LTR) reached new highs in ambulatory surgery (86 out of 100), medical practice (86), inpatient (70.5) and emergency department (69.5) settings through 2025. Overall ratings across each of those settings also improved from the prior year, with the exception of a slight decline (70.4 to 69.7) among inpatient facilities.

Several data points highlighted in the report paint the picture of how inconsistencies or other operational hurdles can impact patients’ reported experiences, and how providers with the best overall satisfaction scores stand out in those areas.

When comparing a planned versus an unplanned admission, for instance, hospitals in the top quartile of overall patient experience scores recorded an 8.9-point median gap between the two encounter types. At bottom-quartile hospitals, unplanned admissions were a median 18.2 points lower.

At the same time, practices that encourage consistent care delivery can make scores for unplanned visits look more like their counterparts. Here, the vendor pointed to bedside shifts, a nursing practice in which nurses going off duty update the on-duty nurse with patient care information at the bedside. A planned admission that did not have a bedside shift was tied to a 68.3 LTR, versus a 76.5 LTR during an unplanned admission that included a bedside shift.

That data point is also an example of the loyalty benefit providers can enjoy when implementing practices to address operational friction, described as a chief drag on patients’ likelihood to recommend a provider. In an inpatient setting, for instance, patients who reported no operational friction rewarded hospitals with LTR scores of 90.6, versus 60.3 when friction is present. These types of operational factors had a greater negative impact on experience scores than those related to clinical care, per Qualtrics’ data.

“The highest performing organizations double down on reliability and consistency, making exceptional experiences the standard, not the exception,” the report reads.

Another standout in the data was patients’ favorable responses to caregivers demonstrating teamwork and trust. Units in the top quartile for teamwork (where patients report “staff worked together for you”) were almost twice as likely to notch top hospital ratings, while those with high levels of trust (as reported by employees) are about 2.4 times as likely to be a top performer.

“Teamwork has emerged as the defining key driver of confidence in care and lasting loyalty,” the report reads. “Patients notice when caregivers communicate clearly, coordinate effectively, and work together toward a common goal.”

Qualtrics’ report concludes with several patient experience recommendations for organizations to target in the coming year. Among these are embracing omnichannel listening, or combining traditional metrics like survey data with other channels; reducing workforce administrative burden to maximize patient face time; and removing barriers that keep patients from making an appointment, including by reserving slots for first visits or by offering assisted scheduling.

#5700. At $12,500, Could This 2004 Nissan 350Z Be Your New Weekend Toy?

With low miles, a six-speed stick, and nothing-rhymes-with-it upholstery, today's Nice Price or No Dice 350Z convertible has a lot going for it as a fun-time car. Let's see how serious we feel about buying it at the seller's asking price.

It's been said—by old Shakespeare, no less—that beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Value, it should likewise be noted, is also a subjective concept. One person's fancy restaurant burger is another's meal budget for an entire week. Mmmm, ramen.

When it comes to cars and trucks, value is rooted not only in price, but also in perceived usefulness and desirability. The seller of the 1999 Ford Expedition XLT that we looked at last Friday asked only $2,600 for it, a mere pittance in today's market. We had to consider, however, not just the dollars, but the desirability of a large SUV like that. Not everybody is keen on something that gets around 12 mpg around town and eyes compact parking spaces the same way Santa looks at skinny jeans. For many of you, that price was too hard to beat, regardless of potential pitfalls. The result was an overwhelming 89% 'Nice Price' win.

Have you looked at a weather report lately? According to meteorologists (which, by the way, is the coolest job title out there next to automotive journalist), North America is about to experience a wet and wild winter, thanks to the Super El Niño now taking up residence in the Pacific. Stormy weather? Wet, maybe slushy roads? That means this might not be the best time to consider buying a RWD, convertible sports car.

Being a community of naysayers, though, and those who forge our own path (usually sideways or backward, spraying a rooster tail of dirt and grass), that's just what we're going to consider. The object of our attention, this 2004 Nissan 350Z convertible, is sufficiently unique in a desirable way to warrant our immediate attention, even if using it to its full potential and driver enjoyment might have to wait until the drier days of Spring and Summer.

Okay, so what's to like about this 350Z? Well, for starters, it's a front-mid engine two-seater with a 287-horsepower naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 under the hood, mated to a six-speed manual. That's a spicy meatball right there. Then there's the convertible top. Yes, not everyone likes unlimited headroom and showing off a Rogaine prescription for all to see, but some do.

As added enticements, the seller claims that the car is completely factory-stock and has a mere 61,000 miles on the clock. That's less than 3,000 miles a year. What a waste!

The reason given for the meager miles is that the car has been used exclusively as a weekend warrior for the past few years, sitting out the work week entirely. As a result, the car is said to be in excellent condition, with a smooth-shifting gearbox and a fuss-free engine. With so few miles under its belt, we have to wonder if it's even on its original brake pads.

Another reason to check out this Z is its almost-new appearance. Painted in dark silver metallic—as were, it seems, 90% of these cars—this Z looks clean and well-kept. The black fabric top is in equally good condition, as are the factory alloys. The tires wrapping those have plenty of tread depth but are cheap-seats Phantom HRX meats which, while not terrible, were probably chosen with the car's sale in mind.

This Z's party piece, however, is its two bucket seats. The rest of the cabin is dullsville black plastic, but the seats, cosseting, modestly-bolstered affairs, are orange-dyed leather with charcoal mesh insets. Those are in great shape, happily showing no wear whatsoever in the pictures. Equally up to snuff are the steering wheel wrap and shift knob, two more leather surfaces. The car has a full complement of comfort and convenience features—cruise, climate control, power windows and locks, etc.—and all are said to work as they should. The cabin also has the added, odd benefit of a factory Bose stereo with both a CD and cassette player built right in.

So far, we've established that this Z puts a lot on the table for an enthusiast to enjoy. Two final incentives: it also has a clean title and the seller's insistence that this is a collectible model.

Known in America as the "Z" or "Z car," Nissan's venerated sports car carried the wonderful Fairlady name in its home market. Over the years, changing market priorities have stunted the Z's U.S. sales. While Nissan has dutifully stuck it out and still sells an updated version of this car today, when was the last time you saw one on the road? In fact, while the company has introduced the new 2027 models, its website still touts that "last year's model year Nissan Z is still available." How sad is that? Maybe the $45K price tag plays a role.

This older, but claimed "like-new" Z asks a far lower $12,500, and it's now time for you all to weigh in on whether that's a fair price or not. What do you think? Is this well-equipped, fantastically upholstered 350Z worth $12,500 as presented in its ad? Or does that price have you thinking about going Rogue?

#5699. Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

Sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue. New research from Florida International University (FIU) has found that several types of sleep disorders are associated with physical changes in brain regions responsible for attention, motivation, and decision-making. These findings suggest that disrupted sleep may be connected to important differences in the brain's structure.

Published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders. The discoveries could eventually help scientists identify sleep problems earlier and develop treatments tailored to the specific brain systems involved.

What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders

An estimated 50 million to 70 million Americans experience sleep disorders, making them a major public health concern. To investigate their effects on the brain, scientists at FIU's Center for Children and Families combined and analyzed findings from 57 studies that used brain imaging to examine adults.

Rather than focusing on a single condition, the researchers compared several sleep disorders to determine whether they were associated with similar changes in brain structure. This approach, which is still relatively uncommon in sleep research, also allowed the team to identify differences specific to certain disorders.

The analysis focused on two broad groups. The first, known as dyssomnias, includes insomnia and sleep apnea, conditions that interfere with falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting sufficient restorative sleep. The second group, called parasomnias, includes sleepwalking, nightmare disorder, and sleep terrors. These conditions involve unusual events or behaviors that interrupt normal sleep cycles.

"As more people recognize how important sleep is, there's growing urgency to understand what's happening in the brain," said Matthew Sutherland, a cognitive neuroscientist at FIU and senior author of the study. "By bringing together results from many studies, this research gives us a clearer picture of how sleep disorders affect brain structure and function and where we need to focus next."

Sleep Disorders Share Changes in a Critical Brain Region

One of the most striking findings was that both groups of sleep disorders were associated with reductions in the thalamus, a structure deep within the brain that plays a central role in processing information, sustaining attention, and supporting complex thinking.

The researchers identified changes in a specific part of the thalamus called the pulvinar. This region helps the brain direct attention toward important information and manage cognitive control, which allows people to regulate their thoughts and actions while completing tasks.

The affected areas are connected to larger brain networks that help people concentrate, make decisions, and respond to their surroundings. Differences in these systems may help explain why people with sleep disorders often experience slower reaction times, difficulty making decisions, and a greater likelihood of errors or accidents.

"Most research looks at sleep disorders one at a time," said Katharine Crooks, a recent FIU cognitive neuroscience doctoral graduate and lead author of the study. "By looking across many studies, we found shared patterns in the brain that help explain why sleep problems can impact focus, decision-making and everyday functioning. With so many people struggling with sleep, understanding what is happening in the brain is key to finding better interventions, diagnostic tools and personalized treatments."

Sleepwalking and Nightmares Show Additional Brain Differences

Although the researchers discovered common structural patterns across sleep disorders, they also found differences associated specifically with parasomnias.

People with these conditions showed changes in the posterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in motivation, decision-making, and the regulation of emotions. This finding may help explain why disorders such as sleepwalking, recurring nightmares, and sleep terrors can sometimes be accompanied by difficulties with mood, behavior, or emotional control.

In contrast, the analysis did not reveal a consistent pattern of structural changes found exclusively in dyssomnias, the category that includes insomnia and sleep apnea.

Together, these results suggest that different forms of disrupted sleep may be associated with both shared and distinct changes in the brain. The particular regions involved may depend on the nature of the sleep disorder.

Could Brain Imaging Lead to Better Sleep Disorder Treatments?

The findings provide researchers with new clues about the relationship between sleep disorders and the brain systems that support everyday thinking and behavior.

By identifying which regions are associated with particular sleep problems, scientists hope to improve diagnostic methods and develop more personalized interventions. Future treatments could potentially aim not only to improve sleep quality but also to protect the brain networks involved in attention, decision-making, and emotional regulation.

However, an important question remains unanswered. The research identified associations between sleep disorders and differences in brain structure, but it did not establish whether disrupted sleep causes those differences, whether existing brain differences contribute to sleep disorders, or whether both processes occur.

To investigate this relationship further, the FIU team plans to examine individual parasomnias in greater detail, including sleepwalking and REM sleep behavior disorder.

Understanding how these conditions relate to changes in the brain could help researchers develop better ways to recognize, manage, and potentially prevent some of the cognitive and emotional difficulties associated with disrupted sleep.

Materials provided by Florida International University. Original written by Rosanna Castro. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5698. What's The First Thing You'd Change If Stellantis Made You Its CEO?

Stellantis is making moves again, this time promoting Tim Kuniskis from merely being the head of its American brands and SRT division to also being its U.S. chief commercial officer. That means Tim's now in charge of the entire dealer network, as well as retail and fleet sales. Since he's in the C-suite, it probably comes with a big raise, too, unlike the promotions that regular people get in America.

Kuniskis isn't European, and it's hard to imagine Stellantis putting an American in charge of its entire corporation, but if anyone could do it, it would be Tim. He's made them a lot of money stuffing big, dumb engines into cars that make big, dumb horsepower, and even if they aren't your cup of tea, it's hard to get too mad at the guy that gave us the Hellcat.

It would be hard to Hellcat all of Stellantis's European brands, but personally, I'd be ok with Fiat building a 700-horsepower 500e. I assume Stellantis CEO Tim Kuniskis would prefer V8s, but if the Fiat's already electric, could he resist building a version that makes big, dumb power? I don't think he could. Because he's Tim Kuniskis, and he likes to go fast.

Similar things could be said about other executives. No matter who hires Johan de Nysschen, you know any good names in the lineup are about to become alphanumeric gibberish. No matter how many vehicles Rivian builds, don't expect RJ Scaringe to offer animal leather as an upholstery option. I bet you have some pretty strong beliefs about the best way to run an automaker, too.

So if you became the next CEO of Stellantis, what's the first change you'd make? Remember, you aren't just in charge of U.S. brands. You're the boss of the whole corporation. Personally? I'd quit. Being any kind of automotive executive seems like a giant headache, and I don't think even a wheelbarrow full of money would make that headache go away. TTHealthWatch is a weekly podcast from Texas Tech. In it, Elizabeth Tracey, director of electronic media for Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore, and Rick Lange, MD, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso, look at the top medical stories of the week.

This week's topics include early-onset colorectal cancer, artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled prior authorization, T cells and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and different metabolic subtypes of adult type 1 diabetes.

0:41 Subtypes of type 1 diabetes in adults

6:16 Increased stromal-to-epithelial ratio

7:50 Was a change in frequency of procedure

10:10 Cerebrospinal (CSF) versus circulation

11:20 Cytomegalovirus interacts with existing conditions

Elizabeth: What are the differences between early-onset colorectal cancer and that that occurs in older people?

Rick: Does AI-enabled prior authorization change clinical practice?

Elizabeth: What's the role of T cells in ALS?

Rick: And different metabolic subtypes of adult type 1 diabetes.

Elizabeth: That's what we're talking about this week on TTHealthWatch, your weekly look at the medical headlines from Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center in El Paso. I'm Elizabeth Tracey, a Baltimore-based medical journalist.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso.

Elizabeth: Rick, why don't we turn to The Lancet? I find this notion of, gosh, subtypes of type 1 diabetes to be pretty intriguing.

Rick: Most often when we talk about type 1 diabetes, we talk about it in kids, and it's an autoimmune disease. There are antibodies that form against the beta cells that cause their death and decrease insulin, and therefore result in diabetes. But the same thing can happen in adults. It looks like there's a lot of different heterogeneity, different clinical presentations. Are these distinct disease entities, or are they just different stages of a shared autoimmune process?

They did a prospective cohort study. They analyzed data from adults aged 18 to 69 that were in the German Diabetes Study that had clinically diagnosed type 1 within the preceding 12 months. And then they asked whether the results were reproducible in a prospective follow-up of the same patients. They assessed different antibodies, their triglycerides, their HDL, and tried to characterize clinical and metabolic subtypes. And then they looked at insulin sensitivity, residual B-cell function, and looked at the trajectory.

And what they discovered is that there were three distinct subtypes. Two had antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase -- I'm going to call it GADA -- and one was GADA-negative. I want to focus on the GADA-positive. They characterized these into two different groups. One was what they called classic type 1 diabetes. These were adults that had a lower BMI [body mass index], high insulin sensitivity, and severe B-cell dysfunction. And the second group that were GADA-positive, they had a higher BMI, lower insulin sensitivity, and they had better B-cell function. They call those the mixed type 1 diabetes.

It appeared that the mixed type 1 diabetes was actually just an earlier form of the classic, about 6 years earlier. If we can identify these individuals, and if we know it's an immune response, perhaps doing immunomodulatory therapy can change things.

Elizabeth: A couple questions about this. I'm always wondering about, gosh, why didn't anyone ever look at this before to see about this heterogeneity, which certainly we see every time we look at something that presents clinically in a certain way. Gosh, there's an awful lot under there; that's that iceberg notion. The other thing is you didn't mention the negative, the other group.

Rick: Yep. It takes a large number of patients, a large amount of data, and you have to do a cluster analysis. And if we take these similarities, then what are the differences between this similar group and that similar group?

Not only are there differences with regard to GADA and the timing of when the diabetes is likely to occur, there was also differences with the risk of hypoglycemia, retinopathy, and cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy. And in fact, they were higher in the mixed group than they were in the classic group.

With regard to the GADA-negative group, had other different antibodies that were responsible for their diabetes. The B-cell function was intermediate between the other two groups. There was a more gradual beta-cell decline, a lower diabetes genetic risk, and reduced islet cell autoimmunity, suggesting it was pathogenetically different and also heterogeneous.

Elizabeth: Clearly, this has important clinical implications and needs to be distilled into something that can be just tested pretty routinely and then employed.

Rick: Yep. When you identify an adult with type 1 diabetes, if we can catch them very early in that disease, when they're in the mixed-diabetes group, we can change their immune system and either delay or prevent progression of the disease.

Elizabeth: Let's turn from here then, speaking of things that happen early in life, to Nature Medicine. And this is a study looking at insights into early-onset colorectal cancer from a single-nucleus RNA-sequencing atlas of colorectal cancer across the age continuum.

What these folks did was they looked at 189 primary colorectal cancer tumors spanning eight decades of life with at least 20 tumors in most age decades. They did a number of analyses on this, stratifying tumors by their microsatellite status, the tumor sidedness in the person, the stage, the patient's sex, neoadjuvant treatment history.

What they found was that tumors from the younger patients were characterized by increased stromal and decreased epithelial proportions. They confirmed that in an external cohort of 712 colorectal cancer tumors. Epithelial cells from the younger patients demonstrated increased expression of what are called long non-coding RNAs, a trend toward increased heterogeneity and copy number alterations. Left-sided colorectal cancer tumors had more cell-to-cell interactions.

What they basically conclude is yes, indeed, there are things that we can look at. This stromal versus epithelial proportion and the sidedness seem to be distinguishing characteristics, and maybe help further understand why this is happening more often in younger people.

Rick: The incidence of colorectal cancer before the age of 50 has been increasing about 1 to 3% per year. It is now the leading cause of cancer death in adults 18 to 49 years of age. Unfortunately, the survival of individuals with early colorectal cancer is poor. This increased stromal-to-epithelial ratio -- there's more connective tissue and less cells -- makes it more resistant to standard chemotherapy. So identifying these individuals early and identifying unique markers that may be more responsive to particular types of therapy are important.

Elizabeth: Clearly points to the need to develop new treatments that are targeted toward these particular characteristics versus the ones that have been classically identified.

Rick: Are these targets of treatment, and are they actually driving the tumor, or are they just bystanders?

Rick: AI-enabled prior authorization and particularly in Medicare.

This is really controversial because prior authorization requires the clinician to submit a justification for a specific medical service. The reason it's controversial is commercial insurers use this as a way of denying insurance and denying payment. If the procedure is necessary, that's really frustrating to the patient and to the physician, obviously. And in the past, Medicare has not required any prior authorizations with rare exceptions.

However, in January of this year, CMS initiated what's called the Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction, called the WISeR model, talking about prior authorization, to make sure that the procedure that's being done is not wasteful and it's not inappropriate because these are services that are considered vulnerable to fraud, waste, and abuse.

So what Medicare said is, OK, we're going to use AI-enabled prior authorization for some particular procedures, one being epidural steroid injection. Before we're going to reimburse hospitals or physicians for this particular procedure, we're going to submit these individuals to prior authorization using AI to do that. Did that really change the use of epidural steroid injection? And by the way, we're going to compare the six states in whom AI authorization was enacted with all the other states.

When they looked at it, the use of AI authorization led to a 15% reduction relative to the baseline use of epidural steroid injection. Did the other procedures that didn't require authorization change? Not at all. Just the ones in whom prior authorization was used. It looked like there was a dip and then there was a recovery. The question is, over the next 6 months, will that maintain or not? Is it just because there's a new process and it slowed things down, and now it's going to recur? Rick: Yeah. You're right. So this is a 6-year project. So we're going to want to follow it for a long period of time. This is just the initial results from the first two quarters, more data to come.

Elizabeth: OK. Turning back to Nature Medicine then, let's take a look at this notion of T cell involvement in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS.

This study is looking at T-cell responses in folks who have it. Previous research has implicated T cells here. And what they're using is single-cell RNA and T-cell receptor sequencing, longitudinal immune profiling, and imaging flow cytometry to identify long-lived intrathecal clonotypes and antigen-presenting T-cell complexes that have features of immunological synapse formation.

What they find is that, sure enough, in the CSF, in the cerebrospinal fluid, they do find these higher frequencies of different subtypes of T cells there that were associated with slower disease progression. Whereas when they noted that these same subtypes of CD4 cells, the T cells, were found in the circulation, they were associated with faster progression of ALS.

They did find that there were also these differences in T-cell clonotypes that were shared between the blood and the CSF exhibited distinct transcriptional states. They also noted that cytomegalovirus-specific T cells in the cerebrospinal fluid and serum antibodies were associated with faster progression and shorter survival in the sporadic form of ALS, which is the majority of the cases, I would note, versus that that's genetically associated. I, at least, am happy to see further characterization of this disease and potentially ways that might point to an intervention.

Rick: Yeah. Neuroinflammation is now recognized as being an important part of the central feature of ALS. About three-fourths of the cases are sporadic, about a fourth are from mutations, and ALS from a complex interplay between both genetic susceptibility and environmental influences that causes neuroinflammation. And, by the way, cytomegalovirus probably isn't the thing that initiates it, it just interacts with all this together. The fact that we can identify different types of T cells, those that regulate or those that help promote inflammation, those different populations in the blood and in the brain hopefully will give us some insight in how best to modulate the neuroinflammation.

Elizabeth: Or even to slow it down. I was gratified to see that the authors of this study did look at other neurotropic viruses and assess their role. So they looked specifically at herpes viruses and they found that this was specific to cytomegalovirus.

One of the questions I have, of course, is that cytomegalovirus is just so very common. What is that interaction? And if it was really a pronounced interaction, I would think that ALS would be a good deal more common than it is.

Rick: Yeah. It's not a uniform driver of pathology, but it interacts with the underlying disease mechanisms. It's a very complicated interplay in terms of the neuroinflammatory response.

On that note then, that's a look at this week's medical headlines from Texas Tech. I'm Elizabeth Tracey.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange. Y'all listen up and make healthy choices.

Google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

#5695. Chutes & Ladders—Mayo Clinic names next CEO; Novant Health CEO to retire

Chutes & Ladders—Mayo Clinic names next CEO; Novant Health CEO to retire" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Welcome to this week's Chutes & Ladders, our roundup of hirings, firings and retirings throughout the industry. Please submit the good news—or the bad—from your shop, and we will feature it here each week.

>Mayo Clinic has announced Matthew R. Callstrom, M.D., Ph.D., as its next president and CEO, taking over for Gianrico Farrugia, M.D., who in May announced plans to step down at the end of the year.

Callstrom, a radiologist, has been with Mayo Clinic since 2002 who is currently medical director for Mayo Clinic Strategy and its AI Program. He's also a member of its board of governors and board of trustees. He's credited for his role in the major nonprofit system's organizational strategy and integration of AI into care.

Farrugia, who has headed Mayo since 2019, plans to stay on through Dec. 31 to ensure a smooth handoff.

>Carl S. Armato, president and CEO of Winston-Salem, North Carolina-based Novant Health, will retire at the end of this year after 15 years leading the system.

Armato joined the nonprofit in 1998 as vice president of finance and operations in its Charlotte and Winston-Salem physician divisions, and held increasing regional and organization-wide leadership roles over subsequent years.

He's credited with boosting access points and unifying Novant's "collection of strong regional organizations into a unified, innovative health system." He also headed substantial growth, with the organization today counting 45,000 employees, 22 hospitals and about 900 total locations.

With his retirement, current Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer John Gizdic will become president and interim CEO on Jan. 1, 2027. His resume includes over 30 years of healthcare leadership, including more than 20 with Novant.

> UnitedHealthcare has named Suha Assi as CEO of individual Medicare Advantage, per a LinkedIn post.

Assi previously spent nearly a decade as executive director for Medicare and Retirement in Tennessee, and she previously held roles based in the state for Cigna. She wrote in the post that the "relationships with our teams, providers and communities have shaped how I think about this business and, most importantly, the people we serve."

"As I step into this national role, I’m excited about what’s ahead for Medicare Advantage," she wrote. "I look forward to working alongside teams and provider partners across the country to modernize how we work together, strengthen relationships, and find new ways to deliver for our members."

> Daryl Tol, president and CEO of General Catalyst's Health Assurance Transformation Company (HATCo) is stepping down from the role, the venture capital firm's CEO Hemant Taneja shared Tuesday.

Tol had been with the firm for about four and a half years in the wake of his time as president and CEO of AdventHealth's Central Florida Division. During that time, he headed HATCo's partner and advisory network—helping grow it to nearly 40 providers, payers and other portfolio companies—and took the company's top spot partway through 2025. Of note, he helped HATCo close its acquisition of regional health system Summa Health and served as its interim CEO for much of the past year until the appointment of Jennifer Eslinger last month.

Tol is being succeeded by Reva Nohria, a founding member of the HATCo team who has been with General Catalyst since 2018. Taneja, in his announcement, said her work at both organizations has encompassed investment, company creation and strategic partnership, and that she will continue as an investor at the venture capital firm alongside her new appointment.

Tol will support a smooth leadership transition and remain in an advisory role, a representative of General Catalyst told Fierce Healthcare.

> Jennifer Shuford, M.D., is leaving her post as deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Nov. 12, just four months after joining, according to a Washington Post report that was confirmed by the agency on Tuesday.

The agency told press in a statement that Shuford was departing "to spend more time with family." Her appointment was announced by President Donald Trump in April, and she joined in June.

Shuford is an infectious disease specialist who came to the federal stage from a role as commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services and before that, served as the state's chief epidemiologist. Notably, she was credited with heading Texas' response to a measles outbreak last year. Her departure comes as the CDC clashes with state health departments and other public health leaders over its response to a growing national measles outbreak.

Satish Pillai, M.D., is slated to fill the role in the interim as the agency seeks a replacement, the CDC said.

> Johns Hopkins Health System CEO Kevin Sowers is set to retire at the end of 2027.

Sowers has served as president and CEO of the Johns Hopkins system since 2018. He also previously spent more than 32 years as a leader within the Duke University Health System, including eight as CEO of Duke University Hospital.

The early announcement of his retirement plans gives Johns Hopkins significant time to conduct a search for a successor, with Theodore DeWeese, dean of the medical faculty and CEO of Johns Hopkins Medicine, leading the charge. Sowers will become a strategic adviser to Johns Hopkins to support the transition, the health system said.

"When I joined Johns Hopkins Medicine in 2018, I made a commitment to the organization and to myself to give 10 years of everything I had to this extraordinary place—to the talented, dedicated people who work here, and the people and communities we serve. And I intend to keep that commitment," Sowers said in a video message.

> Calley Means, a prominent senior advisor to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. closely aligned with the Make America Healthy Again Movement, resigned from his role on Thursday.

The resignation was reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Means on social media.

Media reports from the past several months described Means' frustrations seeing MAHA policy priorities delayed or blunted by others in the administration, with the journal citing sources describing him as "disillusioned." Still, his time advising the secretary notched several wins for the movement, including overhauled dietary guidelines, steps toward greater food ingredient transparency and loosened restrictions on psychedelics as potential medical treatments.

Means wrote in his confirmation post that he still holds "tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy" in their battles against "the entrenched, dark forces in D.C. that profit from Americans getting sick."

"More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past two years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started," he wrote.

> Premier Health, a five-hospital nonprofit academic system in Southwest Ohio, has appointed Rosanna Morris as its upcoming president and CEO, effective in the first quarter of 2027.

Morris is currently executive vice president and chief clinical operating officer at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, and was previously president of Beaumont Hospital-Royal Oak. She is a registered nurse by training and has more than 27 years of health leadership.

She takes over for the retiring Michael Riordan, who has led Premier Health for about half a decade. During that period, he's credited, by the system's board, with stabilizing the system's finances.

> Centivo has added two leaders to its C-suite, the health plan announced.

Lisa Bielamowicz, M.D., will join the company as chief health officer, while James Parr will step into the role of chief commercial officer. Both are veteran healthcare leaders, Centivo said.

Bielamowicz has a long career as a physician and health system consultant, and will take on the chief health officer title after advising Centivo's board of directors.

Parr has previously served as a senior adviser to employers at Lockton as well as senior vice president and head of sales at Collective Health. Parr has also held leadership roles at Cigna, per the announcement.

"There are few leaders in healthcare who have the health benefits strategy knowledge and have built the strong relationships that Lisa and James bring to Centivo," said Ashok Subramanian, co-founder and CEO of Centivo, in the announcement. "These new leaders put Centivo in a strong position as we launch in new markets and help more employers across the country tackle rising healthcare costs and restore affordability by rethinking their healthcare benefits strategy."

> Inspira Health CEO Amy Mansue will be retiring at the end of the year, and will be succeeded by current President and Chief Operating Officer Warren Moore, the four-hospital South Jersey system announced this week.

Mansue will have been at the helm for six years, and is credited by the organization for expanding local care access and championing a culture of wellness among its 7,800-person workforce.

Moore has led Inspira's operations since 2021 and was promoted to president at the top of this year. He has 35 years of industry experience and will most immediately prioritize the opening of a new hospital tower and building upon the system's recent Epic launch.

“Leading Inspira has been one of the great privileges of my career,” Mansue said in the announcement. “I’m proud of what our team has accomplished and grateful for the trust of our communities. After working alongside Warren for many years, I know his ability to bring people together, navigate complex challenges and understand what our patients and neighbors count on us to deliver. I have every confidence in his leadership of Inspira’s next chapter.”

> Joint Commission has named Ken Grubbs as its chief operating officer, effective Jan. 1.

Grubbs is the first nurse to serve as COO of Joint Commission Enterprise in organization’s history, according to the Oct. 13 announcement. He currently serves as the organization's chief nursing executive and executive vice president of Accreditation and Certification Operations.

He will succeed James Merlino, M.D., who will take over as the organization's president and CEO this coming January.

> Beth Israel Lahey Health's national leadership search has yielded Peter Shorett as its next president and CEO. His appointment takes effect this coming January.

Shorett is currently the system's senior executive vice president and chief operating officer, and played a role bringing together its Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute for an upcoming strategic collaboration for cancer care. Prior to joining in 2019, he was a senior partner at Chartis.

He'll be taking over for Kevin Tabb, M.D., who in March gave notice to the system's board that he plans to step down after this year. He'd the role at Beth Israel Deaconess since 2011 and guided the organization through its 2019 merger with Lahey Health.

> WellSpan's Board of Directors has named Laureen Driscoll as the Pennsylvania-based system's new president and CEO.

The executive and registered nurse's appointment will go into effect Jan. 4, 2027. She takes over for Roxanna Gapstur, Ph.D., who announced plans to retire this past spring.

Driscoll is joining the 12-hospital, $4.7 billion nonprofit from Providence, where she currently serves as chief executive for its south division and oversees 17 hospitals with $10.3 billion of net operating revenue. Prior to that she held roles at MultiCare Health System, Swedish Health System, Le Bonheur Children's Medical Center and Maine Medical Center.

“She has led complex health systems through transformation while strengthening quality, culture, access and performance," Board Chair Joe Crosswhite said in the announcement. "Just as important, she leads with purpose and understands that listening to team members, clinicians and communities is essential. The Board is confident Laureen is the right leader for WellSpan’s next chapter.”

> UnitedHealthcare has elevated Bobby Hunter to the role of president at the insurer.

Hunter wrote in a LinkedIn post that in the new position he will be tasked with leading the charge on the company's modernization efforts, including investments in technology and other initiatives to simplify the healthcare experience for its members.

Hunter most recently served as CEO of Government Programs at UnitedHealthcare, and has held multiple leadership roles at the insurer dating back to 2011.

"The future we're working toward is one where plans and providers work together more seamlessly, information flows instantly, trust is earned through transparency and accountability, and care teams are able to spend more time focused on patients," he wrote in the post. "To get there, we must continue to deliver on the commitments we make to the people, providers, customers, and communities who count on us every day."

> Jonathan B. Perlin, M.D., Ph.D., will retire from his roles as president and CEO of accrediting organization Joint Commission on Dec. 31. Current Chief Operating Officer James I. Merlino, M.D., is slated to succeed him.

Perlin boasted three decades of healthcare executive leadership across his career, which included five at the top of Joint Commission. During that period he oversaw a substantial reduction on Joint Commission standards deemed to be burdensome or obsolete, and programs to support healthcare safety issues in low- and middle-income countries. Titles preceding his time at the organization included president of clinical operations and chief medical officer for HCA Healthcare, and the U.S. Department of Veteran's Affairs' under secretary for health.

Perlin will remain a strategic advisor to the group following his retirement, holding the title of president emeritus.

Merlino's career included leadership roles at Cleveland Clinic such as chief clinical transformation officer and chief experience officer, as well as at healthcare performance improvement company Press Ganey.

> Robert C. Garrett, CEO of Hackensack Meridian Health, will retire next year after decades with the organization, including its formative 2016 merger.

Garrett is set to step down on June 30, upon which time he'll hold the role of CEO emeritus for a year to help ease the transition. The 18-hospital, nearly $10 billion nonprofit said it plans to announce his successor before the year's end.

Garrett began his career in the early 1980s at Hackensack University Medical Center, and in 2009 was named president and CEO of Hackensack University Health Network. When the organization merged with Meridian Health in 2016 to form New Jersey's largest health system, he served as co-CEO for two years before taking on the solo mantle.

Alongside the organization's growth to more than 500 patient care locations, Garrett's tenure also marked the opening of the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine, New Jersey's first new medical school in decades.

"Bob has been the driving force behind HMH's unprecedented growth and transformation, its superior quality, innovation and commitment to building an exceptional workforce," Board Chair Keith Banks said in a statement. "At the heart of Bob's legacy is his unwavering belief that we must deliver the most innovative and compassionate care to all patients. HMH is solidly positioned for continued growth, and we are profoundly grateful to Bob and extend our warmest wishes to him for this well-deserved next chapter."

> The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the leading lobbying group for the pharmacy benefit management industry, has named CVS Health executive Ed DeVaney as its board chair.

DeVaney currently serves as president of CVS Caremark, one of the PBM industry's "Big Three" firms. He succeeds Adam Kautzner, president of Express Scripts and Evernorth Health Services, representing one of the other "Big Three" companies.

“The role PBMs play in lowering costs and improving access to prescription drugs for Americans is critically important,” DeVaney said in the announcement. “As Board Chair, I’m committed to ensuring PCMA shares our story with policymakers, consumers and employers so they have a full understanding of the work we do to fulfill our commitment to lower drug costs.”

> UnitedHealth Group has elevated Dan Kueter to serve as the company's chief commercial officer, per a LinkedIn post.

Kueter previously served as the CEO of UnitedHealthcare's commercial business for four years. UHC is the health insurance arm of UnitedHealth Group.

In the new role, Kueter will be tasked with working across both UnitedHealthcare and Optum to support coordination in product development and innovation, he wrote in the post. He said he will also collaborate closely with other senior leaders at the UnitedHealth Group level.

"I'm looking forward to working across the company with colleagues at Optum and UnitedHealthcare to help drive our next chapter of growth and innovation, focused on helping make healthcare work better for everyone," Kueter wrote.

In a separate post, Brandon Cuevas revealed that he will succeed Kueter as CEO of UHC's commercial unit. Cuevas most recently served as executive vice president for the national health plan at Kaiser Permanente, and he previously held multiple leadership roles during a 14-year stint at UnitedHealthcare.

Cuevas said in the post that he "couldn’t be more excited to rejoin a team that is so capable and committed to making positive change in healthcare."

> Optum has named Ujjwal Ratan as the new chief AI officer for its Optum Insight unit, per a LinkedIn post.

In the role, he will be tasked with leading the development of the critical infrastructure that Optum Insight will build its agentic AI toolset on. Ratan has previously held leadership roles at Amazon Web Services and at Oracle, according to his profile.

"Agentic AI only works if the agents have real, connected data to reason over — and few organizations sit across as much of the healthcare journey as Optum does: providers, payers, pharmacy, life sciences and government programs, under one roof," Ratan wrote. "That's exactly the foundation this next wave of AI needs, and exactly why I think Optum is positioned to set the standard for agentic AI across healthcare, not just inside it."

> Association of American Medical Colleges President and CEO David J. Skorton, M.D., will retire from his post on June 30, 2027, the group announced this week. A search for his replacement is currently under way.

Skorton stepped into the role in July 2019 and was kept on by the board in a unanimous 2023 vote. He's credited with guiding the association through the pandemic and overseeing a comprehensive strategic planning process that brought a new vision and mission. Prior to joining he served as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution and was president of Cornell University and the University of Iowa.

“He will be leaving the AAMC an even stronger association than when he arrived," Board Chair Michael Waldrum, M.D., said in a statement. "Identifying a visionary leader to guide the association and the academic medicine community into the future will be our next challenge.”

> Cotiviti, a healthcare infrastructure and data analytics platform, has appointed Erin Schmuker as its chief operating officer.

She enters the role with over 20 years of healthcare leadership, coming directly from a job as president of integrated pharmacies at OptumRx. The new position tasks Schumuker with scaling Cotiviti's operating model, bolstering execution and accountability, simplifying operations and bolstering its growth.

“Our opportunity is to connect data and intelligence to the workflows where decisions are actually made and turn that intelligence into action at scale," President and CEO Ric Sinclair said of the appointment. "Erin is a proven operator who understands how to do that. She knows healthcare, she knows our clients and she knows how to bring people, technology and operations together to deliver results. She will help us move faster, operate better and scale Cotiviti for what healthcare needs next.”

> Kaiser Permanente recently announced that Shaun Smith will be joining as executive vice president and chief people officer, effective Oct. 12.

Smith, who will be reporting directly to the CEO as well as to the president of integrated care and coverage, comes from a chief people and culture officer roles at NewYork-Presbyterian.

> The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA) has named Dan Serrano senior vice president and chief financial officer to oversee the organization’s enterprise financial strategy.

Serrano joins BCBSA after holding leadership roles across the health insurance, provider and value-based care sectors. His experience includes serving as chief financial officer for Aetna's Mid-Atlantic Region and holding senior finance positions at ChenMed, Healthfirst, as well as several other home-based and primary care organizations. He also served as vice president of value and risk-based contracting at Mount Sinai Health System.

“Dan's extensive experience across the healthcare ecosystem, combined with a strong track record of aligning financial performance to operational outcomes, makes him a tremendous addition to our leadership team,” said BCBSA president and CEO Kim Keck in a statement.

>Keck Medicine of USC announced that CEO Rodney Hanners will be stepping down on Sept. 24, alongside a handful of other leadership changes at the system and its affiliated Keck School of Medicine of USC.

Hanners was in the role for six years, a period in which he extended the Los Angeles-based organization's reach into Pasadena and the San Gabriel Valley.

Taking over for him will be Steven Shapiro, M.D., currently senior vice president for health affairs, who joined in 2021 from a run as president of the University of Pittsburg Medical Center.

The university noted that it will be trimming the role's responsibilities, reverting supervision of some USC health science schools to the provost "to allow Steve to focus more intensely on elevating our academic medical enterprise."

Beneath him, the university has also named Chief Clinical Officer David Peng, M.D., as deputy executive vice president for health affairs and Keck Medical Center of USC CEO Marty Sargeant as chief operating officer of the broader system. Both Peng and Sargeant will remain in their prior roles alongside the new responsibilities.

USC's announcement also included word that Keck School of Medicine of USC Dean Carolyn Meltzer is stepping down for a new role as president of the Radiological Society of North America. Vassilios Papadopoulos, dean of the university's pharmaceutical school, will be filling her role on an interim basis.

>Health tech company Health Catalyst appointed Simeon Kohl as Chief Executive Officer and President and a member of the company’s Board of Directors, effective September 14.

Kohl most recently served as CEO of Performant Healthcare, a public healthcare company he led through significant strategic and operational transformation, culminating in its sale to Machinify for approximately $670 million. He brings more than 20 years in healthcare, spanning operations, growth and public company leadership. The company’s current CEO and President, Ben Albert, will become Chief Business Officer and will step down from the Board of Directors effective September 13.

During his tenure, Albert led Health Catalyst's strategic priorities and operating initiatives and aligned the leadership team now running the business. He sharpened the company’s focus on its highest-conviction technologies, positioning Health Catalyst as an AI-forward healthcare intelligence company, executives said.
