#5649. Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk

Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning. A long-running study of U.S. adults suggests that drinking caffeinated coffee regularly is associated with a substantially lower risk of dementia and better cognitive health as people age.

Researchers found that adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee developed dementia at considerably lower rates than those who rarely or never drank it. The findings were based on follow-up periods extending as long as 43 years, offering a valuable look at how everyday drinking habits relate to brain health over time.

The strongest associations appeared among people who drank two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day. Tea consumption was also linked to better cognitive outcomes, although the amount associated with the greatest benefit was somewhat lower.

Interestingly, decaffeinated coffee did not show the same benefits, raising questions about whether caffeine itself might help explain the connection.

Coffee Drinkers Showed Much Lower Dementia Rates

One of the most striking findings involved the difference in dementia rates between regular coffee drinkers and people who consumed little or no coffee.

Among U.S. adults who drank higher amounts of caffeinated coffee, researchers recorded 141 dementia cases annually for every 100,000 people. In comparison, the rate was 330 cases per 100,000 people each year among those who rarely or never drank caffeinated coffee.

Dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with memory, thinking, reasoning, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer's disease is its most common cause, although several other brain disorders can also lead to dementia.

While occasional forgetfulness can be a normal part of aging, dementia involves cognitive difficulties severe enough to disrupt daily life. Identifying lifestyle habits associated with lower dementia risk is therefore an important area of research, particularly as populations grow older.

The findings suggest that regular caffeinated coffee consumption may be one such habit. However, the results show an association rather than proving that coffee directly prevents dementia. Other differences between coffee drinkers and people who avoid coffee could also contribute to the observed results.

Coffee Was Also Linked to Better Cognitive Health

The potential benefits were not limited to diagnosed dementia. Participants who drank more caffeinated coffee were also less likely to report that their memory or thinking abilities had declined.

Researchers found that 7.8% of adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee reported subjective cognitive decline, compared with 9.5% of those who rarely or never drank it.

Subjective cognitive decline refers to changes in memory or thinking that people notice themselves, even when those difficulties have not necessarily been confirmed by formal cognitive testing. Someone experiencing it might feel that remembering information, concentrating, or finding the right words has become more difficult.

Such complaints do not automatically indicate dementia. Nevertheless, they can provide useful information about how people perceive changes in their cognitive abilities as they grow older.

The lower percentage among caffeinated coffee drinkers adds to the evidence linking coffee consumption with healthier cognitive aging.

How Much Coffee Offers the Greatest Benefit?

The researchers also examined whether the amount of coffee consumed was related to the strength of the observed benefits.

Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with the most favorable outcomes for dementia risk and cognitive functioning.

Notably, this association remained apparent regardless of participants' genetic risk of developing dementia. In other words, the relationship between coffee consumption and brain health was observed even among people whose inherited characteristics might make them more vulnerable to the disease.

Genetic risk refers to the influence of inherited variations in DNA that can increase or decrease a person's likelihood of developing certain conditions. Although genetics can play an important role in dementia, they are only one part of a much larger picture that includes age, general health, and lifestyle.

The results also suggest that drinking larger amounts of coffee is not necessarily better. Consumption beyond the range associated with the strongest benefits did not appear to provide additional protection.

Tea Drinkers May Benefit Too, but Decaf Was Different

Coffee was not the only beverage associated with better brain health. Researchers found that drinking tea was also linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning.

For tea, the strongest associations appeared among participants who consumed one to two cups per day. As with coffee, drinking more than this amount did not appear to produce further benefits.

However, the study did not distinguish between caffeinated and noncaffeinated tea. As a result, the findings cannot establish whether caffeine was responsible for the association observed among tea drinkers.

The results for coffee offered an additional clue. While regular caffeinated coffee was associated with lower dementia risk and better cognitive outcomes, decaffeinated coffee did not demonstrate the same benefits.

Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee, tea, and several other plants. It acts on the central nervous system and is best known for temporarily increasing alertness and reducing feelings of tiredness.

Whether caffeine also contributes to better brain health over many years is a separate question. The difference between regular and decaffeinated coffee makes this possibility worth investigating, but it does not establish caffeine as the cause of the observed benefits.

Taken together, the findings suggest that moderate consumption of caffeinated coffee and tea may be associated with healthier brain aging. For coffee drinkers, two to three cups daily appeared to offer the strongest association, while one to two cups of tea showed the most favorable results among tea drinkers.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these beverages directly influence dementia risk, the long-term findings offer encouraging news for people who already enjoy coffee or tea as part of their daily routine.

#5648. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5647. Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.11% Rate

Mortgage rates continued their slow retreat for a fourth consecutive week, mirroring the trajectory of bond yields, although this week's hotter-than-expected inflation print suggests the relief will be short-lived.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans decreased to 7.11% for the week ending Nov. 12, down 7 basis points from 7.18% the week before, according to Freddie Mac. Even with this steady month-long decline, borrowing costs remain significantly higher than they were a year ago, when rates averaged 6.24% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

At today's 7.11% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,314. This reflects a $16 monthly reduction from the previous week’s payment of $2,330.

Compared to the 6.24% average from November 2025, which required a $2,116 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $198 more every single month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.11% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,791.

This reflects a $20 decrease from last week's monthly cost of $2,811. Compared to the 6.24% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,552, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $239 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $193 in relative relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this continued downward drift improves overall borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.11% rate will pay a total of $833,080 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage. While current financing costs remain elevated compared to year-ago levels, this total still represents a distinct contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $57,550 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.11% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,004,902 for principal and interest. If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $69,421 for FHA buyers.

While stubborn inflation may limit how much further rates can fall in the weeks ahead, this four-week pullback has helped trim monthly expenses for buyers jumping in the late-fall market.

Welcome to Chief Complaint, a new STAT+ column from Frances Mei Hardin, M.D. A former ear, nose, and throat surgeon, she writes about the many challenges facing those who practice medicine in a time of great change.

During my second year of residency, my husband drove me to the batting cages for the first time. He’d noticed I was coming home with an increasing level of rage, with nowhere for it to go. I had never swung a bat before, but we spent an hour that evening in a netted room, him slow-pitching and me swinging out of my shoes. My hands stung and my bones shook with every hit, but it was the best that I felt in months.

This batting cage salve is about the only type of “physician self-care” that ever actually worked for me, and it didn’t come from a hospital-mandated wellness module, nor a doctor appreciation pizza party. What actually gets prescribed to physicians is basic wellness fare: the mindfulness worksheets, the resilience webinars, the optional yoga in unused office room C in the old hospital annex building.

#5645. BeOne, Hengrui top list of China’s most powerful drugmakers

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Reporter at Large, Live and Feature Journalism

Damian covers the global drug industry and contributes to STAT’s industry-leading events. You can reach Damian on Signal at damiangarde.67.

China’s ascendant drug industry is no monolith, despite how it’s often described by Western competitors, pundits, and policymakers. The country is home to scores of companies with diverging ambitions, founded last year or last century, each vying for attention and capital amid a domestic scientific renaissance and a geopolitical standoff.

It’s complicated. To help make sense of it, STAT and the risk intelligence platform WireScreen on Monday published China’s Biotech Powerhouse 25, a ranking of the country’s most valuable publicly traded firms that tracks the varying strategies — and fortunes — of the world’s rapidly growing new medicine chest.

The list’s top-ranked firms typify China’s rise to prominence on the global stage and the forking paths to get there.

At No. 1 is BeOne Medicines, formerly known as BeiGene, a company founded in 2010 to straddle East and West that has become one of the first Chinese firms to build a worldwide sales operation. In second place is Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals, which began nearly 60 years ago as a state-owned generics firm and has evolved into the partner of choice for Western pharma giants looking to in-license promising new medicines. One company seized on the need for new cancer medicines to establish a commercial beachhead in the U.S.; the other has capitalized on the gold rush for potential blockbusters developed swiftly and efficiently. Each is worth nearly $50 billion as a result.

The rankings — and attendant scores given to each company — are based on two equally weighted metrics: market value and revenue. Companies are put on a scale of 0 to 50 compared to the leader on each of the two measures, meaning a company leading both would get 100. Only Chinese firms whose primary business is discovering novel medicines for human disease were eligible, meaning the list includes no contract research firms, pharmaceutical service providers, or generics companies.

STAT and WireScreen plan to update the rankings each quarter as licensing deals, product launches, and market forces affect the fortunes of the country’s emerging powerbrokers.

Beijing has made biopharma a national priority, aiming to produce at least a quarter of the world’s first-in-class drugs by 2030 and host at least 50 domestic companies worth $1 billion or more. Washington and even the biotech industry itself are hung up over how to respond, caught between an impulse to demand what would amount to molecular import controls and pharmaceutical companies that want to keep shopping for low-cost intellectual property from Chinese labs.

Last month, the Trump administration moved to block certain deals between U.S. firms and Chinese drugmakers, proposing controversial changes to a law called COINS, short for the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act. Given President Trump’s unpredictability and the political shift in Washington set to take place following the midterm elections, no one’s certain of how the policy landscape might be affected.

“The relationship between nations is pretty dynamic, where Trump can have a productive meeting with President Xi and then turn around and put out a rule on COINS,” said Leonid Timashev, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets who covers biotech.

Many in the U.S. drug industry are advocating for policies aimed at accelerating domestic drug development, not curtailing progress in China. John Crowley, president and CEO of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization, sees China’s biopharmaceutical ascension as grounds for a modern-day Space Race, one that demands the U.S. bolster its research spending, speed up the process of running clinical trials, and incentivize companies to make their drugs in America.

“The next century of biotechnology leadership is not destined to belong to any nation,” Crowley wrote in STAT. “It will be earned by the nation with the vision to invest, the courage to innovate, and the resolve to build the future.”

By most metrics — number of clinical trials, research spending, patents filed — that nation is China. But, as each update of the Powerhouse 25 is likely to illustrate, the Chinese biotech industry only prospers if all that work turns into drugs that work in the clinic and sell on the market.

#5644. Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins

A major clinical trial has raised new questions about how doctors decide who should take statins to prevent heart attacks and strokes. Researchers found that using heart scans to guide treatment decisions produced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, even though the scans led to far fewer recommendations to begin taking statins.

The findings, presented during a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026, also revealed a striking difference in how consistently patients took their medication. Those advised to use statins based on calcium buildup in their coronary arteries were substantially more likely to follow their treatment recommendations.

Although the results suggest that heart scans could help doctors make more targeted treatment decisions, the trial did not establish that the scan approach was as effective as conventional risk assessment. Researchers say additional studies are needed to determine whether it offers a better strategy for preventing cardiovascular disease.

Why Predicting Heart Disease Risk Remains a Challenge

Cardiovascular disease remains the world's leading cause of illness and death. Much of this burden comes from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), which develops when fatty deposits known as plaque accumulate inside arteries, restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Coronary artery disease and ischemic stroke are two major forms of this condition.

Several common factors increase the likelihood of developing ASCVD, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, and elevated cholesterol. Doctors use these factors to estimate a person's cardiovascular risk and determine whether preventive medications are appropriate.

Statins are among the most widely used treatments for lowering that risk. These medications reduce cholesterol levels, particularly low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called LDL or bad cholesterol. They also help lower the likelihood of serious cardiovascular complications.

However, identifying which patients stand to benefit from statins remains a significant challenge. Some people who eventually experience a heart attack do not appear to be at particularly high risk under conventional screening methods.

"For far too many patients, the first symptom of ASCVD is a heart attack," said Doctor Joseph B Muhlestein from the Intermountain Medical Center, Murray, USA, the Principal Investigator of the CorCal Outcomes trial. "Statins have been shown to be highly effective in the prevention of ASCVD; however, there is a major gap in risk assessment, statin initiation, and statin persistence."

According to Muhlestein, many people who suffer their first heart attack, particularly younger adults, would not previously have been classified as having enough cardiovascular risk to justify statin treatment. This limitation has prompted researchers to investigate whether directly examining the arteries might provide more useful information.

Can Heart Calcium Scans Improve Statin Decisions?

The CorCal Outcomes trial investigated two different approaches for determining which patients should be advised to begin statin therapy before experiencing a cardiovascular event.

The first relied on the pooled cohort equations (PCE), a commonly used risk assessment tool that estimates cardiovascular risk using traditional factors such as age, cholesterol levels, blood pressure, and smoking status.

The second approach measured coronary artery calcium (CAC), which provides a more direct indication of plaque buildup in the arteries supplying the heart.

This measurement uses a computed tomography (CT) scan to detect calcium deposits in the coronary arteries. Calcium can accumulate within atherosclerotic plaque, making it a useful marker of underlying coronary artery disease, even in people who have not developed symptoms.

Unlike traditional risk calculators, which estimate the likelihood of future cardiovascular problems based on personal characteristics and health measurements, calcium scans provide evidence of disease already present in the coronary arteries.

Researchers wanted to determine whether using this information to guide statin recommendations could improve cardiovascular outcomes.

Nearly 5,800 Patients Put Both Methods to the Test

The trial enrolled 5,772 patients from the Canyons and Desert regions of Intermountain Health Care in the United States. Participants had no known history of ASCVD or diabetes and had not previously received statin therapy.

Their average age was 64, and women accounted for 51% of the study population.

Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to one of two groups. One group received statin treatment guidance based on traditional cardiovascular risk scores, while the other received recommendations based on coronary calcium scan results.

Both patients and their physicians were informed of the treatment recommendations generated by the study protocol. However, the final decision about whether to start taking statins remained with the patients and their doctors.

The researchers then tracked major cardiovascular events (MACE; all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and arterial revascularization).

This combined outcome included death from any cause, heart attacks, strokes, and procedures to restore blood flow through narrowed or blocked arteries.

Heart Scans Led to Far Fewer Statin Recommendations

After an average follow-up of 4.2 years, researchers found that major cardiovascular events occurred at exactly the same observed rate in both groups.

A total of 2.7% of patients in each group experienced one of the events included in the study's primary outcome. The estimated relative risk over time was also nearly identical (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% confidence interval 0.71 to 1.38; p=0.045 for noninferiority).

However, this similarity did not establish that the two strategies were equally effective. The study failed to meet its predetermined statistical requirement for demonstrating that the calcium scan approach was not meaningfully worse than conventional risk assessment.

A notable difference emerged in how frequently patients were advised to begin taking statins.

Participants evaluated using traditional risk scores received recommendations to start statin therapy more than three times as often as those whose decisions were guided by coronary calcium measurements.

Despite this substantial difference in treatment recommendations, both groups experienced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events during the follow-up period.

A Surprising Difference in Statin Adherence

Perhaps the most intriguing finding involved whether patients actually followed their prescribed treatment.

Among those advised to take statins, patients whose recommendations were based on calcium scans were much more likely to adhere to their medication regimen than those assessed using traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

The difference was substantial (62% vs. 23%).

In other words, patients recommended statins based on visible evidence of calcium buildup in their arteries were approximately 2.7 times as likely to follow their medication regimen.

One possible explanation is that seeing evidence of disease in their own arteries makes patients more motivated to take preventive medication. However, the trial did not establish why adherence differed so dramatically between the groups.

The findings raise the possibility that coronary calcium scans could influence not only which patients receive statin recommendations, but also whether those patients consistently take the medications.

What the Findings Mean for Heart Disease Prevention

Despite these potentially important differences, the researchers emphasized that the study could not establish whether calcium scan-guided treatment provides cardiovascular protection comparable to traditional risk assessment.

One important limitation was that fewer participants experienced major cardiovascular events than the investigators had anticipated. With fewer events to analyze, the trial had less statistical power to determine whether a meaningful difference existed between the two approaches.

"The power of the study to detect a difference was reduced by the lower-than-expected event rates and we did not demonstrate noninferiority between the groups," said Doctor Muhlestein, who concluded: "The study did provide important hypothesis-generating insights into the efficiency of statin initiation and adherence when decisions are based on CAC scoring. Taken together, our data could be used to plan an additional well-powered randomized trial comparing CAC with current risk factor-based algorithms."

The findings may help researchers design future trials capable of determining whether coronary calcium scans can improve the efficiency of statin prescribing without compromising cardiovascular protection.

Current European recommendations already recognize a potential role for these measurements. The 2025 Focused Update of the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidemias recommends considering increased coronary calcium scores, when available, as an additional factor in cardiovascular risk assessment.

This guidance applies particularly to people at moderate cardiovascular risk or those whose estimated risk falls near the threshold at which preventive medication would normally be recommended.

For these individuals, evidence of calcium buildup may help doctors make more informed decisions when the need for statin therapy is uncertain.

The CorCal Outcomes findings add to the discussion by suggesting that heart scans may also influence how faithfully patients follow treatment. Whether that advantage translates into better long-term cardiovascular outcomes remains an important question for future research.

Not only do these unique properties offer a place to call home but they also provide a chance to preserve a piece of the past while creating something entirely your own.

Full of charm, character, and possibilities, these structures feature many original details, including vintage bank vaults and architectural details.

From Maine to Wisconsin, we found five converted banks and schoolhouses priced below $400,000 that offer a unique opportunity to live somewhere with a story to tell.

CSAA Landmark Schoolhouse: Built in 1865, this 600-square-foot building has been converted into a stylish one-bedroom, loft-style home.

The charming open floor plan has hardwood floors and a cozy living room that flows into the dining area and kitchen. A spiral staircase leads to the sleeping quarters, which have vaulted wood ceilings. Recent improvements include energy-efficient hydronic baseboard heating.

Built in 1901, this property features a vintage bank vault, original ATM, night-deposit box, glass block windows, and private offices. #5642. After difficult two years, medical school group’s leadership isn’t letting its guard down post midterms

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

ANAHEIM, Calif. — After spending a tumultuous two years entangled in many of the most consequential health and science policy debates of President Trump’s second term, the Association of American Medical Colleges isn’t ready to let its guard down after Democrats won control of the House and Senate.

That was one of the core messages delivered to the 4,100 medical educators, research heads, clinicians, and trainees who convened earlier this month for its annual meeting here in Southern California, just a short walk from Disneyland and California Adventure. For a few surreal days, walking along palm tree-lined streets and beneath a cloudless sky, you were just as likely to pass a medical school dean as a family of four in matching Mickey Mouse ears.

Inside, standing before a packed conference hall, AAMC Chief Public Policy Officer Danielle Turnipseed ticked through the nonprofit’s many policy battles since January 2025, from fighting reductions to National Institutes of Health funding to concerns around Medicaid cuts to proposed visa fines and restrictions that would affect international physicians and researchers. She stressed that a Democrat-led Congress won’t mean that these or other issues will go away.

“The work still remains,” Turnipseed said. “By no means do the issues that we talked about fade away: How physicians are paid, how our hospitals are supported, how student financial aid issues are resolved. And there are so many new people to meet on both sides of the aisle.”

To better understand how AAMC’s leadership views this moment, STAT sat down with CEO David Skorton, a cardiologist and former president of Cornell University and the University of Iowa. Skorton, who is retiring next June, said he was hopeful lawmakers would continue to reject attempts by the Trump administration to place grant decisions under political control, and that they’d seriously consider a proposal to modernize how the federal government pays for research overhead, also called indirect costs. He also expressed optimism that bipartisan support for biomedical research will continue despite Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), a prominent Republican advocate, losing her reelection bid.

But he pointed to rising medical mistrust as a lasting underlying issue, citing AAMC’s own surveys on the topic. The findings underscored that, in many cases, mistrust is fueled by memories of times when organizations have not been trustworthy.

“I do not blame the public at all for that,” he said. “I believe that trust needs to be earned.”

The following conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

How has the current political climate shaped the tone and content of this year’s meeting?

There are uncertainties in every aspect of our world, whether it’s research funding, medical education, student loans, immigration issues. A quarter of the practicing physicians in the country are international medical grads. In some disciplines, it’s much higher than that. And certain things that are happening in the administration and in Congress in the last year or so have put financial strain or the threat of financial strain forward. For all those reasons, I think people want to be together, want to discuss things in an open way, and we’ve tried to plan the sessions to cover those issues.

There’s a whole session track on “biomedical research and discovery in changing times.” Speaking of change, how does the Democratic takeover of Congress affect your outlook on policy areas that are important to AAMC?

I’m hopeful that we can get on with doing the research and spend less time arguing about the ground rules. But I do think that some of the stuff falls on us. For example, in the area of facilities and administrative costs, indirect costs, we need to be more transparent and clear about how those are audited. We’re part of this Joint Associations Group that has developed this thing called the FAIR model [which would require institutions to directly account for certain overhead expenses in project budgets]. I think that will be at least potentially more transparent, not only to the general public, to voters, but to the people in Congress and in the administration. Time will tell.

Congress has blocked the White House Office of Management and Budget from putting grant reviews more directly under political control, but that restriction ends Dec. 11. Do the midterm results give you confidence those changes won’t take effect?

Even though the overall Uniform Guidance change is halted by the continuing resolution for another month, I am concerned that there’s sufficient evidence that they are trying to make some of these changes agency by agency, which would be a more indirect way of doing the same thing. I think this is a very big mistake, and that’s why we came out so strongly against the change. We’re a nonpartisan organization, and it’s my job to work with the administration [and] both sides of the aisle. Nothing about this election changes the principles on which we operate, or what we’re aiming for.

Are you concerned that Collins losing her Senate seat will make it harder to find Republican support for research funding?

She was a very strong — is a strong champion for us. But in general, it’s been bipartisan support. I’m not cocky or overconfident or anything like that. But this time I’ll use the word optimistic that this will continue to be bipartisan support because it helps everybody. … I think people don’t disagree about the need for it because there’s too many unsolved problems.

The political winds ebb and flow, and I’ve been around a long time in many different leadership positions. I’m most concerned that the election in ’24 and public polling suggest that we have lost a lot of the trust of the public, both as researchers [and] as clinicians. … We have an organization called the Center for Health Justice. They do national polling in communities. We asked the community members when we first set up the organization six years ago, “What can we do to educate the public so they’ll trust us?” And their [first] answer, which is on our website, is, “We’re already educated. That’s why we don’t trust you.”

I believe that’s what we need to work on, what we can do to put our house in order to earn people’s trust. That will reflect itself in politics, in policies.

#5641. Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction

A new national study suggests that the way people consume cannabis may reveal important clues about their likelihood of using it heavily or developing an addiction. While smoking remains the most popular method among US adults who use cannabis, roughly one in seven consumes it in nearly every available form. Researchers found that this group had particularly high rates of daily use and cannabis use disorder.

Cannabis is consumed in several ways, including smoking, vaping, eating edibles, and dabbing, which involves heating concentrated cannabis products and inhaling the resulting vapor. Its use is widespread in the United States. Recent national survey figures indicate that approximately 43.8 million Americans ages 12 and older (more than 15 percent) had consumed cannabis within the previous 30 days.

Researchers at NYU Langone Health identified four distinct patterns of cannabis consumption. Nearly half of users, 48 percent, primarily smoked cannabis, while 21 percent combined smoking and vaping. Another 17 percent mainly consumed edibles. The remaining 14 percent belonged to what researchers called the "polymodal group," meaning they used cannabis in almost every available form.

Cannabis Addiction Rates Differ Sharply by Consumption Pattern

The findings, published online August 8 in the journal Addictive Behaviors, revealed major differences in how frequently these groups consumed cannabis. Approximately half of people in the polymodal group reported using it every day. Daily use was considerably less common among other participants, occurring in 28 percent of those who primarily smoked, 31 percent of those who smoked and vaped, and about 13 percent of those who mainly consumed edibles.

An even more striking difference emerged when researchers examined cannabis use disorder, the medical diagnosis associated with cannabis addiction. About 67 percent of polymodal users met the criteria for the disorder, compared with 47 percent of those who both smoked and vaped, 36 percent of those who mainly smoked, and just 15 percent of participants who primarily used edibles.

"Our findings suggest that using cannabis in multiple forms may be a red flag for heavier use and symptoms of addiction," said study lead author Omar El-Shahawy, MD, PhD, MPH, an assistant professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. "Asking patients not only whether but how they use cannabis could help clinicians identify when a fuller assessment may be warranted."

To investigate these patterns, the research team examined responses from 17,732 adults who had used cannabis during the preceding month. The information came from the 2022-2023 National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Using statistical methods to identify similarities in participants' consumption habits, the researchers conducted the first national analysis of how different methods of cannabis use naturally group together.

Younger Adults More Likely to Use Multiple Forms of Cannabis

The researchers also discovered notable differences in the characteristics of people who preferred particular consumption methods. Young adults ages 18 to 25 accounted for nearly one-third of both the smoking and vaping group and the polymodal group. In contrast, only about one sixth of participants who primarily smoked cannabis belonged to that age range.

Edibles showed a different demographic pattern. Women made up more than half of those who mainly consumed edible cannabis products, and this method was particularly common among college graduates. However, the study did not investigate what motivated participants to choose specific consumption methods, leaving the reasons for these differences unresolved, according to Dr. El-Shahawy.

Another finding raised concerns about the potential effects of inhaling smoke. People who smoked cannabis were more likely to also smoke cigarettes than those who mainly vaped cannabis or consumed edibles. Because both tobacco and cannabis smoking involve combustion (burning), people who regularly smoke both substances may expose their lungs to additional harmful chemicals.

"The strong tie between smoking cannabis and smoking cigarettes is of concern because this subset of people are breathing in a wider range of chemicals via combustion, and their lungs are at risk," said senior author Joseph J. Palamar, PhD, MPH, a professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

Why Cannabis Prevention Messages May Need to Change

The findings suggest that health education should account for the different ways people consume cannabis rather than concentrating primarily on smoking. Different consumption patterns may call for different approaches to explaining potential risks, particularly among younger adults and people who regularly combine several methods.

"Public health messages about cannabis still focus mostly on smoking, but people now use the drug in many different ways," said Dr. El-Shahawy. "For younger adults, that means talking about the risks of vaping and combining multiple forms, while for people who prefer edibles, the message is to 'start low and go slow' because the effects take time to kick in."

The researchers hope to investigate the motivations behind these consumption patterns in future work. According to Dr. El-Shahawy, one question is whether people who favor edibles are more likely to use cannabis to manage problems such as pain or difficulty sleeping.

The team also emphasized several limitations. Because participants described their own cannabis habits, some may not have reported their consumption accurately or completely. The observational study also cannot determine whether using multiple forms of cannabis directly increases addiction risk. It establishes an association between consumption patterns and cannabis use disorder, rather than proving that one causes the other.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health through grant R01DA055675.

Additional NYU Langone researchers who contributed to the study included Mohsen Abbasi-Kangevari, MD, MPH; Michelle He; and Xiaoying Zheng, alongside Drs. El-Shahawy and Palamar. Neal Doran, PhD, of the University of California, San Diego, also served as a study co-investigator.

#5639. Rates Come Down Again but Remain Over 7%

wood block of percentage change to UP and Down arrow. Interest rate, GDP, stocks market, financial, deflation and Inflation, ranking, mortgage, debt, Loan and Economic Recession concept

Mortgage rates eased again for the fourth-straight week but remain almost a full percentage point over last year at this time, a key reason buyers continue to hold back and why the market remains sluggish.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Thursday shows the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate at 7.11%, down seven bases points from  7.18% last week. The 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year from 6.24% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.45%, down from 6.57%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.49%.

At presstime, the average rate was back up to 7.42% Thursday afternoon, according to Mortgage News Daily.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said that while rates are at their lowest level since late September, borrowing costs are still nearly a full percentage point higher than they were last year at this time.

“While rates have declined for three weeks in a row, homebuyers are still holding back,” Sturtevant said in a statement. “Higher rates, along with on-going economic uncertainty, are key reasons why housing market activity is so sluggish this fall.

She also said there is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year, and that, given this week’s inflation report, it’s more likely for rates to increase instead.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines,” she said. “In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets. Inventory is rising but higher rates are causing sellers to pause along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly even if rates move higher.”

Sturtevant noted that data on pending home sales suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the fourth quarter. “It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

Realtor.com Senior Economist Jiayi Xu added that the recent downtrend trend with rates could potentially reverse next week as the 10-year yield returns to 5%.

“The strong October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Fed’s next rate hike,” Xu said in a statement. “On Tuesday morning, before the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger 50-basis-point move should be considered in December’s meeting if inflation came in hot. Shortly afterward, the October CPI report came in hotter than forecast, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%. A December hike is now essentially priced in. The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast.”

Xu also said today’s homebuyers are being squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, with inflation being the bigger long-term problem.

“High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are,” she said. “But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated. Inflation also leaves households with less to put toward a home, especially when wages lag prices. First-time buyers feel it most. With no equity to lean on, they must save a down payment from budgets already stretched thin. Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years.”

“A price cut tells you the seller’s first number did not work. It does not tell you what the home is worth,” says one real estate professional. “Some reductions create a legitimate opportunity. Others simply bring an unrealistic price closer to where it should have started.” Read more.

#5638. Opinion: Medical school should start after students take the Step 1 exam

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Fabi and Caruso Brown are bioethicists at SUNY Upstate Medical University.

This article is the first in a new First Opinion series on redesigning medical school.

There are more than 150 medical schools across the United States, and although each has a unique approach to medical education, all must grapple with certain challenges. Attendance at in-person lectures and learning sessions hovers around 50% across the country. Students increasingly rely on expensive commercial resources to prepare for their board exams, much to the dismay of their faculty. Meanwhile, students are taking on increasing amounts of debt to finance their four years of medical school.

It’s time for a radical reimagining of medical education. We propose separating medical education into two parts.

Part one would encompass the foundational, preclinical sciences that are tested on the U.S. Medical Licensing Exam Step 1, which students typically take during or just after after the second year of medical school. Part two would include everything else that is critical to becoming a medical doctor: clinical skills and clinical reasoning, professional identity formation, deeper dives into ethics and population health (beyond the bare basics tested on Step 1), and learning in clinical spaces.

Instead of learning the crucial content of part one in medical school, students could take individual pathways to master the content. Rather than requiring students to enroll in an M.D. program to learn the foundational sciences, part one could take many different forms to suit a variety of learners and institutions. This could include a DIY approach, in which a student pieces together available prep materials (Anki, UWorld, etc.) on their own timeline and takes Step 1 when they are ready, at an estimated cost of less than $2,000.

Alternatively, students could take packaged Step 1 courses, online and/or asynchronously, which would perhaps be equivalent to a certificate course, for an estimated $5,000-$10,000.

A third option could be to enroll in a one-year online master’s degree in biomedical sciences, for an estimated $10,000-$25,000.

Yet another option might be for undergraduate schools to offer official “pre-medical” bachelor’s programs that prepare students for Step 1.

Finally, schools could offer a one-year in-person master’s degree, ideally with guaranteed acceptance to the institution’s M.D. degree program following passage of Step 1. At more than $30,000, this would likely be the most expensive option.

At the end of whichever part one preparation pathway a student chooses, they would sit for the Step 1 exam and apply for medical school after passing. It is worth noting that the USMLE itself responds to the question “How do I prepare for the test? Is there a review book for USMLE?” without mentioning medical education, instead emphasizing review of the content online, practice examinations, and self-assessments.

Part two of medical education, which would begin after passage of Step 1, could also take different forms. This training could include two years of classroom instruction on how to be a doctor, potentially tied to pre-acceptance into certain residency slots in order to encourage students to enter specific high-needs specialties. Alternatively, part two could take three years and include time for research or a capstone project alongside education in doctoring.

The arguments for reimagining medical education to move foundational sciences from the M.D. curriculum to a pre-admission period are many. Perhaps most importantly, the cost of medical education has increased over 80% since 2001, adjusting for inflation. At the same time, the federal government is now capping federal direct unsubsidized loans at $50,000 annually and $200,000 total, putting four years of medical school out of reach for many students. For medical students who struggle and have to repeat a year in the preclinical curriculum, this financial burden is even more significant. Adding in the cost of external Step 1 study resources, which students often pay for out of pocket on top of their tuition, makes medical education in our current model even more prohibitively expensive. Moving part one of medical education out of the traditional medical school setting could save these students from untenable amounts of debt.

The debt concern also interacts with the not insignificant number of students who do not currently pass Step 1 on their first attempt (9% of students in 2024 and 7% of students in 2025 — around 2,000 students annually). Failing Step 1 even once reduces a student’s chance of matching, and may mean they cannot go into the specialty that was their major motivator for entering medical school in the first place.

The students may also incur more debt if they have to take a leave to study and retake the exam, and given that pass rates drop with each retake, some of these students may never pass, leaving them with very few career paths open to help recoup the debt they’ve incurred. Even “compassionate off-ramp” programs — still a rarity — often leave students with significant educational debt and without a clear pathway to a high-income career. By making Step 1 passage a prerequisite for entering medical school, institutions can circumvent this possibility.

Having a variety of part one pathways could additionally diversify the applicant pool. A flexible timeframe for studying for and passing Step 1 might allow people to work and/or support and raise a family before entering the more rigidly structured part of medical school.

Similarly, a lower financial bar and degree of investment in preclinical education might make it more accessible.

Of course, this would require equitable access to part one preparatory materials, curricula, and biomedical sciences programs. That could happen through a free clearinghouse of publicly accessible materials and scholarships to access privately available ones. If these necessary components of part one preparation are financially out of reach for some prospective medical students, the plan might actually reduce the diversity of admitted medical students.

Our proposed restructuring of medical education might also help to decrease the stigma in residency applications associated with multiple attempts at Step 1 — but again, if stigma is not reduced by this approach, then this might further advantage good test-takers, who often come from affluent backgrounds, over other students.

Another argument in favor of this new model of medical education is the positive effect it could have on the quality of education, by enabling schools to allocate teaching resources more effectively. We strongly believe that medical school should be about learning how to be a doctor, not how to pass a test, but currently many students prefer packaged commercial test prep materials to the courses their schools are offering. This is a misuse of resources that reflects a misalignment of values, particularly when many students report that they do not value in-person class time and watch lectures on 2x speed.

M.D. programs have made efforts to address this disconnect by incorporating early clinical exposure and education in areas not emphasized on Step 1, such as ethics and structural competency. But these efforts also miss the mark when students remain preoccupied with passing the exam, rather than absorbing the lessons about how to be a compassionate, well-rounded physician.

We experience these challenges firsthand in the ethics and health systems sciences courses we teach, as medical students in our classrooms visibly choose not to engage with our course materials, opting instead to review flashcards from external Step 1 study sites. Restructuring medical education to begin after Step 1 might allow schools the flexibility to reallocate resources required to implement time-variable, competency-based clinical training, wherein students advance through training based on the acquisition of core skills, rather than completion of a certain number of weeks on a given rotation.

Such approaches are effective but resource-intensive, requiring a shift in resources from preclinical to clinical training. For example, foundational sciences faculty might be re-deployed as coaches to help support students who are struggling to apply foundational knowledge to clinical reasoning.

And indeed, the type of competency-based overhaul of medical education would inevitably require time, resources, and very careful planning to assure that it doesn’t create other undesirable eventualities. Medical schools might reasonably be concerned that this move could negatively affect students and faculty if implemented without proper consideration of the risks.

It’s certainly possible that our proposal might lead the content of Step 1 to shift into undergraduate college courses, driving students to focus narrowly on a “pre-med” major that becomes increasingly intensive and competitive, an outcome we consider undesirable. However, this could be mitigated by additional restrictions on the timing of Step 1: Say, for instance, a requirement that students enroll in a clinical undergraduate medical education program within one year of passing. State medical licensure requirements (i.e., that all Step components be passed within a seven-year old period) might also help to avoid this outcome.

We haven’t worked all the kinks out of this. This proposal would create other logistical puzzles in need of solutions: do osteopathic medical schools follow suit? How would this affect the timing of application and admissions cycles? What would be the role of the MCAT going forward? What would happen if more students pass Step 1 than can be admitted into medical schools? How would M.D./Ph.D. and other Medical Scientist Training Programs (MSTPs) be reorganized?

We acknowledge the scale and breadth of these potential complications, and we invite our colleagues in medical schools across the country to join us to imagine creative ways to improve and renew our approach to educating our nation’s future physicians.

Rachel Fabi, Ph.D., and Amy Caruso Brown, M.D., M.Sc., are bioethicists at SUNY Upstate Medical University. Fabi also writes the daily STAT mini crossword. Views presented here are their own and do not represent the views of their institution.

The First Opinion series on redesigning medical school will run through the end of 2026. Have an idea for a big or small way to change medical school? Email us.

#5637. A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

Researchers have identified a protein that may play an important role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin. The discovery could provide a promising new target for treatments designed to improve blood sugar control.

The protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes. In preclinical experiments, scientists discovered that removing Miro1 restored the muscles' response to insulin. They also found that exercise lowered Miro1 levels in people with the disease, offering new insight into how physical activity improves insulin sensitivity.

The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.

How a Hidden Muscle Protein Affects Insulin Resistance

Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) is located on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells responsible for producing energy. Researchers believe that excessive amounts of this protein may interfere with how muscles respond to insulin, making it more difficult for the body to regulate blood sugar effectively.

To investigate this connection, the research team studied Miro1 in laboratory cells, preclinical models, and people living with Type 2 diabetes. By examining the protein across these different settings, they were able to explore its effects on muscle function and determine whether the findings could be relevant to human disease.

The results showed that Miro1 buildup impaired the muscles' response to insulin. When researchers removed the protein in preclinical models, insulin responsiveness returned, providing evidence that Miro1 contributes directly to this process.

Exercise Reduces a Protein Linked to Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also investigated whether exercise could influence Miro1 levels in people with diabetes. In a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care.

People assigned to the exercise group experienced a decline in Miro1 levels in their muscles. These changes occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles' capacity to produce energy.

The findings suggest that reducing Miro1 may be one of the ways exercise helps the body respond more effectively to insulin. They also raise the possibility that treatments designed to target the protein could eventually provide additional benefits alongside physical activity.

"Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle's response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it," said Dr. John P. Kirwan, the study's senior author.

A Promising New Direction for Diabetes Treatment

Kirwan recently became executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma. He carried out the research while working at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and has since brought his internationally recognized translational research program to the University of Oklahoma.

He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the university and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

The study's first author, Elizabeth Heintz, is a doctoral candidate who worked in the Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory at Pennington Biomedical. Christopher Axelrod, the study's co-corresponding author, has also moved to the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, joining Kirwan in continuing this line of research.

Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical, emphasized the importance of connecting laboratory discoveries with research involving patients and broader populations.

"This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health," said Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. "Dr. Kirwan and his team's findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment."

Could Targeting Miro1 Lead to New Diabetes Therapies?

Although the results are encouraging, scientists still need to establish whether directly targeting Miro1 can produce safe and effective treatments for people with Type 2 diabetes. The restoration of insulin responsiveness was demonstrated in preclinical models, while the human trial showed that exercise reduced Miro1 levels alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity.

Kirwan plans to continue investigating these findings at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. His research will combine laboratory experiments with studies involving people to uncover more of the biological mechanisms responsible for diabetes and explore new strategies for preventing and treating the condition.

"Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally," he said. "Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution."

The study received funding from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

#5636. Detached Home in Desirable DC Neighborhood Gets Major Discount—and the Photos Hide a Wild Catch

A Washington, DC, home has been put on the market for far under the area’s median listing price, but the reason is buried within the listing—and online forums are not happy about it.

At first glance, 1007 Evarts St. NE is a stunning six-bed, five-bath home with a jaw-dropping $375,000 price tag, nearly 40% below the ZIP code’s median listing price of $607,500.

The first nine photos on the listing show an updated, bright, and beautifully staged home with a perfectly manicured lawn. But flip to the 10th photo, and the image changes. The rest of the photos show a smaller home, stripped to the studs and in need of complete rehabilitation, both inside and out.

The key detail then becomes clear: a watermark reading “Architect’s rendering—not an actual photo” in the corner of the listing’s primary photos.

The property details tell the rest of the story.

“Much of the pre-construction work is already done. Demolition is complete and the structure is down to a clean shell with the framing exposed,” the property details read. “The sale includes a DC-approved plan set for a full rebuild. The renderings in the photos show the finished home as designed.”

Investors, developers, and 203(k) rehab buyers who want to skip the design stage and jump right into construction are the ideal buyers, according to the listing.

With that information taken into consideration, the severe price reduction from the area’s norm listing makes sense.

However, the listing has still received heat online, where one Threads user reposted the images with the caption, “This has got to be the most click bait home ive ever seen…..this gotta be illegal, right?”

The replies are filled with equally outraged users.

“Is that AI renderings of potential build and then the actual pics of an as-is shack???” wrote another user.

“The listing is deceptive because you don’t know what you’re looking at. I certainly don’t. And you’re right, you can’t advertise potential. It’s absolutely unethical,” wrote one user, who identified herself as a real estate agent. “The architect rendered pics should have never been included. Those would easily be shown separately to a potential buyer. If you’re selling a clean shell, that’s all that should be pictured.”

The listing did have one defender in the replies: the home’s listing agent, Tohmai Smith. He argued that all of the necessary information is available in the listing, and if he was trying to deceive buyers, pictures of the house as is wouldn’t have been included.

“It’s in the description: ‘The renderings in the photos show the finished home as designed.’ And they’re not AI. A licenses architect built them from the DC-approved plans, which convey with the sale,” Smith wrote. “The finished home is a $1.3M house. The $400K buys you the shell, the approved plans and a head start.”

Users continued to question his claim that the photos weren’t made with AI, pointing out discrepancies in the rendered photos and structural issues with the back staircase as potential clues that they weren’t made with professional architectural programs.

Others questioned the possibility of fitting a six-bed, five-bath home on the moderate 5,066-square-foot lot.

In subsequent replies, Smith explained the use of 203(k) loans to both buy a home and finance the renovation in one mortgage and further argued that the purpose of the renderings is to show buyers the home’s potential. Within these posts, he invited interested parties or those with questions to send him a direct message.

“Without these renderings, how would a buyer know what’s possible? Even after seeing them, people can’t believe it,” Smith wrote. “But it IS possible, and that’s exactly why I show them.”

Bright MLS, which is responsible for listings in the mid-Atlantic region and carries the Evarts Street listing, has a rule that any “virtually staged” images must be labeled, and no AI alterations can alter permanent features or hide defects, according to Imagen for Real Estate.

Another law has been proposed in Washington, DC, to require listings to disclose any photo editing and include both unedited photos and a written list of all changes.

Despite online controversy, the listing for 1007 Evarts St. NE appears to follow both the active and proposed guidelines, by including actual photos of the property and describing the state of the home in the property details section.

Realtor.com reached out to both Smith and Bright MLS for comments on the use of renderings in listings, but received no response at the time of publication.

#5633. Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

Protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

"It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," says Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences."

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity

Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

Experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

Human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an important indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

Research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching new highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

These effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

Studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

Researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging

The amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an important role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially important: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

Research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming says.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

Pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

This distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming says. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are."

The findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
